title: Cloudflare's Growth Keeps Accelerating — the Stock Is Priced for Perfection
subtitle: Q2 revenue climbed 35.9% to $696.1 million with a $60 million guidance raise, three straight quarters of acceleration, and a record 4,698 large customers. The catch: insider selling into the pop — and a forward multiple near 180x.
summary: Cloudflare delivered its third straight quarter of accelerating growth in Q2 2026: revenue rose 35.9% to $696.1 million, full-year guidance jumped by $60 million at the midpoint, and large-customer count hit a record 4,698. AI-driven demand is real — but with the stock near 180x forward earnings and insiders selling into the pop, the valuation leaves no room for error.

bodyHtml:
For the better part of a decade, Cloudflare's pitch to Wall Street was simple: build the network first, monetize later. The patience is beginning to pay off in a hurry. The company's second-quarter report, released Thursday after the close, showed revenue growth accelerating for the third consecutive quarter, powered by an AI-driven demand cycle that is lifting the entire cybersecurity sector. The numbers were strong enough to send shares surging roughly 15 percent in after-hours trading — and pointed enough to raise an old question: whether the market's enthusiasm has finally outrun the fundamentals.

The Numbers That Matter

The headline numbers were hard to argue with. Revenue came in at $696.1 million, up 35.9 percent year over year and roughly 4.7 percent ahead of consensus — a beat that would have been impressive at any size. Management responded by raising full-year revenue guidance by about $60 million at the midpoint, to a range of $2.864 billion to $2.870 billion. That implies the second half of the year is expected to be just as strong as the first, and the market heard the message loud and clear.

The growth is broadening, not just deepening. Large customers — businesses spending more than $100,000 a year — reached a record 4,698, up 27 percent from a year ago, with 986 net additions over the trailing twelve months. Cloudflare is no longer merely a developer tool that enterprises tolerate; it is becoming infrastructure they depend on. The mix of new logos and expanding spend from existing accounts is the healthiest possible signature for a subscription business at this stage of its life. Beneath that sits a developer base expanding even faster: 7.4 million developers now build on the platform, and 2 million of them signed up in the second quarter alone.

The AI tailwind is the engine. More than half of the requests now crossing Cloudflare's network are generated by machines rather than humans — bots, AI agents, and automated services rather than fingers on browsers. Every AI agent that scrapes a website, calls an API, or runs a workflow is a potential customer, because somebody has to manage, rate-limit, and secure all of that machine traffic. The Workers platform has become a default home for AI applications, and each one needs the security and performance layer Cloudflare sits on. It is a toll booth for the machine economy — and the machine economy is growing fast.

The beat itself was not a fluke. This is the third consecutive quarter in which growth has accelerated, and the guidance raise suggests the momentum is compounding rather than fading. The customer additions were spread across industries rather than concentrated in a handful of AI winners, exactly what investors want to see from a company this size. In short, the operating story is about as clean as it gets.

Then comes the part that gives value investors pause. The stock's pop was met with a wave of insider selling: Chief Executive Matthew Prince disposed of roughly $45 million in shares, and Chief Financial Officer Thomas Seifert about $15.6 million, both under pre-arranged 10b5-1 plans. Insider sales into strength are rarely a bullish signal, even when scheduled. The company also reported a GAAP net loss of $170 million, driven by a $150.7 million restructuring charge — the cost of repositioning the business, management says, not a symptom of demand weakness. And the valuation leaves no margin for error: at roughly 180 times forward earnings, with the stock now trading above the average analyst price target, the market is pricing every future quarter to be as good as this one.

The bull case writes itself: Cloudflare is executing better than it ever has, growth is accelerating while many peers decelerate, and AI is creating durable new demand for its network. The bear case is just as simple: the stock is priced for near-perfection, insiders are selling into strength, and the restructuring charge is a reminder that even fast-growing companies make painful choices. Both cases are true at the same time. For long-term believers in the machine economy, Cloudflare remains one of the best-positioned names in cybersecurity — but for anyone looking for a margin of safety, this is not the quarter, or the price, where you will find one.
